questions.q: How is held-out preference accuracy measured?
options: The average absolute score the model assigns to chosen candidates
The fraction of held-out pairs where the model scores the chosen candidate higher than the rejected candidate
The number of held-out pairs the model refuses to score
The training loss on the held-out set
questions.explain: Preference accuracy counts how often r_chosen > r_rejected on pairs the model never saw during training.

questions.q: What was this project's held-out preference accuracy on the regular (non-adversarial) held-out pairs?
questions.explain: On the 42 regular held-out pairs, the model scored the chosen candidate higher 83% of the time.

questions.q: How is the adversarial subset specifically constructed?
options: By randomly duplicating existing training pairs
So that surface polish and real information preservation deliberately disagree — the 'rejected' candidate looks tidier but has silently dropped real information the 'chosen' candidate preserved
By removing all Phone fields from every record
By using only rows from a single country
questions.explain: The adversarial pairs are built to isolate whether the model relies on polish or on genuine information preservation, by making the two signals conflict on purpose.

questions.q: What accuracy did the reward model achieve on the adversarial subset, and what does that reveal?
options: 95%, showing the model is extremely robust
83%, identical to the regular held-out set
48%, close to chance, revealing a surface-polish bias where the model often favors tidy-but-information-losing candidates
0%, showing the model always picks the wrong candidate
questions.explain: The sharp drop to near-chance performance on the adversarial subset reveals that the model partly learned to associate tidiness with quality rather than genuine information preservation.

questions.q: Why is the surface-polish bias described as a 'generalization failure' rather than a labeling error?
options: Because the training pairs were mislabeled according to the rubric
Because the training pairs were labeled correctly per the rubric, but the model picked up a correlated, easier-to-detect surface signal instead of the deeper signal the rubric actually prioritizes
Because the adversarial pairs were labeled incorrectly
Because DistilBERT cannot represent information preservation at all
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the training data was labeled correctly — the issue is that the model learned a correlated but less reliable signal (polish) instead of the rubric's top-priority signal (information preservation).
